Boufeldja Benabdallah, l’homme derrière: Boufeldja Benabdallah, the man behind the public figure
Boufeldja Benabdallah revient sur son pa: Boufeldja Benabdallah looks back on his journey between Algeria and Quebec, his community involvement and the memory of January 29.
Ce portrait est né du désir de comprendr: This portrait grew out of a desire to understand who the man is behind the public figure that many Quebecers know through his work at the Centre culturel islamique de Québec, the January 29, 2017 attack and the debates on secularism.
Pour réaliser ce texte, j’ai suivi Boufe: To write this piece, I followed Boufeldja Benabdallah in January 2026 during the three days of commemoration of the attack. I observed him in different settings: at the official ceremonies, as well as in his exchanges with families, citizens, elected officials and journalists.
Nous avons ensuite eu une longue convers: We then had a long conversation at La Boîte à pain, right across from the Centre culturel islamique, followed later by a phone call. Each time, we went back over his childhood in Algeria, his arrival in Quebec, his international career, his commitments and his family life.
Ce type de portrait fait partie du trava: This kind of portrait is part of the work we aim to do at La Converse: presenting trajectories that are often little documented in Quebec media, spotlighting figures from immigrant and racialized communities, and showing what their journeys say about Quebec, its transformations and the bonds being built here.
‍<strong>Au Québec, le nom de Boufeldja: ‍In Quebec, the name Boufeldja Benabdallah almost instantly evokes the same constellation of references: the Centre culturel islamique, January 29, 2017, a measured voice in a debate that rarely is. He is credited with restraint, a capacity for dialogue, a kind of quiet steadiness in the face of polarization. But the man himself overflows on all sides. His story doesn't begin with the attack or with the visibility that followed. It takes root in Tlemcen, in western Algeria, and unfolds over several decades and several continents, through twists and turns that nothing really foretold.
À La Boîte à pain, où il a ses habitudes: At La Boîte à pain, where he is a regular, Boufeldja Benabdallah is already seated, waiting for our meeting. His posture is upright despite his age, his suit sober, his gaze sharp behind thin glasses; his presence gives off a sense of calm. In some photos, notably <l1>alongside Justin Trudeau</l1>, he is seen smiling broadly, warm and almost familiar. Over more than two hours of interview, that same availability keeps returning: he listens at length, then answers precisely, taking the time to go back over details. His voice is steady, sometimes punctuated by a discreet smile, sometimes carrying an emotion he makes no effort to hide.
Ce jour-là, la boulangerie est animée. L: That day, the bakery is bustling. Conversations overlap, orders follow one after another. He stays focused, as if creating a zone of calm around himself. The place sits across from the Centre culturel islamique de Québec, on chemin Sainte-Foy, and recalls another, much heavier scene.<l1> On January 29, 2017, after the attack</l1>, worshippers took refuge here and were welcomed spontaneously by the owner. He speaks of it as a gesture that is never forgotten – an immediate human response to violence.
Boufeldja Benabdallah est né en 1948 à<l: Boufeldja Benabdallah was born in 1948 in<l1> Tlemcen</l1>, Algeria. He puts little emphasis on dates, more on places and atmospheres. The neighbourhood where he grew up is very old, made up of narrow alleys and houses built using techniques inherited from Roman times. “Solid bricks, laid horizontally and diagonally to give strength,” he describes, as if travelling back in time.
Sa famille est modeste. Il évoque un mél: His family was modest. He mentions a mix of<l1> Amazigh</l1>, Arab and Mediterranean origins, without making it a central element of his identity. “All of that makes North Africa a place of blending,” he sums up. Above all, he speaks of a land crossed by influences, languages and histories.
L’enfance est également marquée par le s: His childhood was also shaped by scouting, which he discovered after <l1>Algeria’s independence in 1962</l1>. The experience structured him deeply. “Living one year of scouting is like living 10 years in civilian life,” he says. The camps, the travel, the collective learning: all of it broadened his horizons well beyond Tlemcen. He crisscrossed the country, discovered its regions, grasped its contrasts. This early mobility gave him a certain ease with moving around that would resurface later.
L’indépendance, justement, reste un repè: Independence, for that matter, remains a strong landmark. He speaks of it as a moment of rare intensity, almost unreal. “We celebrated for a week. I didn’t even go home anymore.” Behind that sentence is a generation in transition, moving from colonial domination to a sovereignty still to be built.
À 21 ans, il quitte l’Algérie pour la pr: At 21, he left Algeria for the first time and landed in Canada, where he had won a scholarship. In the late summer of 1969, he arrived first in Montréal, then made his way to Quebec City to study forestry and geodesy at Université Laval.
Le début se fait sans transition. À son: The start came with no transition. When he arrived on campus, his room wasn’t ready. What could he do, not knowing anyone? An employee suggested he try a nearby church. He went, knocked on the door and was welcomed by a nun, who offered him a room and let him settle in. He would stay there for a week, fed and housed, with nothing asked in return. That welcome would mark him forever. “I was completely happy to see such generosity,” he says. The episode comes up often in his story. Not as an anecdote, but as a starting point. A first concrete experience of what he would later call hospitality.
The rest followed, layer by layer. Summer first, then autumn, which he describes as “a fairy-tale spectacle.” The maples, the colours, the campus surrounded by woods. Then winter, harsher, but not entirely foreign. In Tlemcen, he says, snow exists, even if it doesn’t fall in the same quantities.
À l’université, son intégration est rapi: At university, he integrated quickly. His math skills surprised his classmates, “especially when there were physics, math, strength of materials classes… all the calculations, I was playing with them,” he recalls. Quebec students embraced him and exchanges multiplied, in class and outside it: theatre, outings, discussions. He picked up local expressions and shared his own. A back-and-forth took hold.
Mais il ne parle pas encore d’appartenan: But he doesn’t yet speak of belonging. “I felt like a guest who has everything in his hands,” he says. The word “home” seems too strong to him at that moment.
La nostalgie apparaît progressivement. E: Nostalgia crept in gradually. It grew more insistent on specific occasions: religious holidays, periods of fasting, family events he couldn’t attend. The link with Algeria then came through letters.
Il décrit un rituel précis : dans l’entr: He describes a precise ritual: in the entrance of his residence building, a row of metal mailboxes. The student always slowed his pace there, then made a gesture that became a reflex: look, check, wait... and most of the time, his box was empty.
Lorsqu’une lettre arrive, l’émotion est: When a letter arrived, the emotion was immediate. “When I read, it ended in tears,” he confides. His family’s words, the greetings, the news: everything brought him back to a distance that couldn’t be closed.
« Il reste toujours un petit quelque cho: “There is always a little something that is fundamental and that you can’t find again in the country that welcomed you,” he says, speaking of family atmosphere, smells, voices. Quebec offered opportunities, study conditions, stability, but for the young student, a part of reality remained elsewhere.
À La Boîte à pain, l’entretien avance, r: At La Boîte à pain, the interview moves forward, paced by memories and silences, when something unexpected happens. At the next table, three people in their fifties are chatting. A woman, seated facing Mr. Benabdallah, seems to be listening in at times. Then she gets up, hesitates only slightly and approaches, simply asking whether he is indeed Boufeldja Benabdallah.
Quand il acquiesce, elle se présente. Il: When he says yes, she introduces herself. They met, she says, several decades ago, when her father worked in the timber industry. No sooner are the words spoken than something changes. Faces light up, eyes meet differently, and memory suddenly opens, releasing warm memories of friendship.
L’un des deux hommes à sa table, son frè: One of the two men at her table, her brother, joins them. He too recognizes the name, the places, the eras. Very quickly the sentences tumble out, names of countries surface, fragments of journeys are pieced back together. They talk about work sites, travel, a time when the roads led all the way to Algeria. The brother and sister then recount those trips, made with their father, across the country. The landscapes, the stops, the impressions left by those stays come back in precise detail. “Wonderful memories,” she says, almost as a matter of course.
Autour de la table, le temps se contract: Around the table, time contracts. What belonged to a distant past suddenly becomes present. The conversation spills over, crosses generations, connects trajectories that nothing seemed destined to bring together here.
<strong>Retours, bifurcations et carrièr: Returns, turning points and an international career
Après ses études, Boufeldja Benabdallah: After his studies, Boufeldja Benabdallah returned to Algeria intending to settle there. He worked in forestry and took part in projects related to the fight against desertification, notably in the Djelfa region. He came of age at a moment when the country was seeking to structure its resources, to experiment, to produce knowledge.
Parallèlement, sa vie personnelle évolue: At the same time, his personal life evolved. In Quebec City, he met a Quebec student, whom he married, and together they decided to settle in Algeria. His family’s reception was tense at first given this unexpected marriage, then things changed quickly. “They found an extraordinary person in my wife. She was adopted, and my father adored her, even though he didn’t speak French,” Mr. Benabdallah recalls. But the context complicated things. Regional tensions, the demands of military service and cultural distance weighed on the couple’s balance. A few years later, returning to Quebec became necessary.
La suite de son parcours est moins visib: The rest of his career is less visible, but remains formative. He began an international career in the timber industry. He worked on projects in Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia, and led programs and negotiations.
Il décrit une période intense, faite de: He describes an intense period made up of nonstop travel, hotels, quick decisions. “I was always living out of a suitcase,” he sums up. He helped develop projects, build networks, move resources around. The experience enriched his outlook, but took him too far from his family. “My wife was very unhappy. I also had three children, so I came home.”
C’est aussi au cours de cette période qu: It was also during this period that he took part in a scientific collaboration that would help bring stevia, a sugar substitute, to a wide audience. Mandated as part of exchanges between Quebec and Chiang Mai University in Thailand, he met researchers who were looking for an alternative to opium poppy cultivation in the Golden Triangle region. He facilitated their visit to Quebec laboratories in Saint-Hyacinthe and Montréal. “From that moment on, the world knew stevia,” he sums up.
Parallèlement, le contexte international: Meanwhile, the international context was changing. Wars, crises, tensions involving Muslim-majority countries. In Quebec’s public spaces, the questions multiplied. “You Muslims… why?” He regularly found himself in the position of having to answer, explain, contextualize.
À vrai dire, il se mêlait déjà de politi: Truth be told, he was already dabbling in politics back at university. “We did politics without being politicians,” he says. The debates were sometimes heated, even tense with certain professors, he recalls, and his positions were firm. A way of entering the public sphere that foreshadowed his future role.

Au fil des années, son engagement commun: Over the years, his community involvement widened. He took part in founding the Centre culturel islamique de Québec, which became a cornerstone for the region’s Muslim community. Besides being a place of worship, the space plays a social, educational and cultural role.
Puis survient l’attentat à la mosquée de: Then came the Quebec City mosque attack – and the turning point. The event thrust him, in spite of himself, into the centre of political and media attention. He became a voice that is listened to, sought out, expected. Since then, his participation in public debate has had one constant: avoiding escalation, maintaining a space for dialogue, reminding people of the complexity of personal journeys.
Aujourd’hui, Boufeldja Benabdallah racon: Today, Boufeldja Benabdallah tells his story without trying to soften its contradictions. His memories move from Algeria to Quebec, from business travel to community commitments, with constant back-and-forth between eras and places.
Mais à mesure que l’entretien avance, un: But as the interview goes on, one thread keeps returning: Algeria. The country he left in 1969 remains present in the way he speaks, in the details he holds on to, in the emotion that eventually takes over his voice. The landscapes, the family, the atmospheres, the smells: everything still seems close, despite the decades and the distance.
À la fin, les phrases ralentissent. L’ém: At the end, his sentences slow down. The emotion becomes harder to contain. As if, behind the public figure shaped by years in Quebec, the young man who left Tlemcen one day with a study scholarship and the idea of coming back remained intact.
